newsitem.title: USA: Mine exploration cash may level off in '97 - Yorkton.
newsitem.headline: Mine exploration cash may level off in '97 - Yorkton.

text.p: Investment in mine exploration will be sharply higher this year than in 1995, but the flow of cash into hunting down new deposits may soon start to level off, said Frank Giustra chairman and chief executive officer of Yorkton Securities Inc.

"The opportunities for finding an elephant-sized deposit is fuelling this boom -- the desire to find the big one," Giustra said. There was scope to find a major base metals or gold deposit each year for the next five years and more.
Yorkton estimated that $3.5 billion was raised for exploration in 1995, and will be "significantly higher" this year, probably $4 billion to $5 billion.
"I suspect were are near the end of the bull market. If it ends, it will be more difficult to raise more, certainly by junior mining companies," Giustra said. "We may level off here slightly."
Even if the current bull market ends, Giustra sees a five- to 10-year trend of strong exploration spending.
Canadian-based Yorkton recently opened a New York office to tap U.S. capital more easily. The company has raised C$2 billion in equity for junior mining companies over the past three years.

The boom was ignited by the end of the Cold War which helped to open up large parts of the globe to exploration outside traditional mining areas of North America, South Africa and Australia. A big surge in Canadian capital markets then fueled the hunt for new deposits.

Unknown penny stocks such as Diamond Fields Resources, Barrick Gold, and Bre-X Minerals were catapulted into the big league. But for each success story, there are several juniors who fail, Giustra cautioned.
"But the amount of money available to this sector has increased dramatically. It's still coming in. There is certainly an appetite," Giustra said.

The big drop in some base metals prices, copper in particular has tumbled following the Sumitomo scandal, and gold's failure to stay above $400 an ounce, does not put off the key institutional investors, especially the mutual funds.
"That's a normal commodity cycle that we are going to have, regardless," Giustra said. "The investors don't look at the day to day performance of the commodity, but 5 to 8 years ahead."

The institutional investors try to spot and buy shares in junior exploration companies, hoping a major mining house will eventually be attracted to buy the junior out, thereby boosting the share price.
Or in the case of Bre-X, the junior is set to become a major producer and the shares are re-evaluated by the market, Giustra said.

"Gold is definitely the darling - the bulk of exploration today in the world is in gold. The potential returns for gold stocks are higher than in base metals," Giustra noted. "In base metals, copper seems to be the only one that's of real interest at this time, but nickel also to some extent."
Diamond exploration is also a big draw at the moment.

Giustra said the coming favorite for mining exploration is the Former Soviet Union, after Latin America and later Africa and South East Asia enjoyed much of the investor's attention in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
